Setting up of Fisheries Development Board 
*61.      SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR:  
 SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government propose to set up Fisheries 
Development Board for overall development of this sector specially the inland 
fisheries; 
(b) if so, its location and time-frame within which it would be set up; 
(c) what is the extent of poaching in our waters by foreign trawlers; and 
(d) the action plan of Government to control this menace? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) and (b) 
The feasibility of establishing a National Fisheries Development Board is under 
examination. 
(c) Poaching by foreign fishing vessels in Indian waters is mainly 
confined to Andaman and Nicobar Islands and to some extent in Palk Strait 
and Gulf of Mannar, Gujarat and off Sand-heads. 
(d) Poaching by foreign fishing trawlers in Indian waters is controlled by 
Indian Coast Guard under the powers delegated to them in the Maritime Zones of 
India (Regulation of Fishing by Foreign Fishing Vessles) Act, 1981 and the Rules 
framed thereunder. Regular patrolling including night patrolling is being maintained 
by Coast Guard ships and aircraft to control poaching. 
Vaccination and immune system 
*62. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the vaccination weakens the immune system; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government have made any research in this regard; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the action taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTHAND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMDOSS): (a) to (e) According to IC MR, there are no scientific studies 
which indicate that vaccination weakens the immune response. 
8 

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Scientists at National Institute of Immunology have done research and not found 
any general weakening of the immune system in response 1 to vaccination. 
Neither have other researchers in other parts of the world made such findings. 
Vaccination apart from being administered for preventive purposes is also 
administered for life saving treatment; Iike for dog bite, snake bite, yellow 
fever, typhoid etc. 
Vaccination is one of the most cost effective public health intervention for 
diseases control. Globally, it is estimated that three million lives are saved 
annually on account of vaccination. It is a process where immunity is acquired by 
introduction of various antigens or antibodies. A vaccine is composed of one 
or more antigens of the pathogens which induces protective immune 
response. 
There are adequate provisions under Drugs and Cosmetics Act & Rules 
framed thereunder for pre-clinical and clinical studies before marketing 
approval is granted for any vaccine. This includes evaluation of toxicity, reacto-
genicity and Immuno- genicity of vaccine. Besides these, there are strict 
requirements of Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) for production of 
vaccines. Licensing of vaccine in the country, has further been brought within 
the purview of Central Licensing. There are elaborate mechanism of consultation 
with experts to ensure safety, efficacy  and quality of all vaccines in the 
country.

Stroke due to drugs given for cold 
*66. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be'pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that pills and syrups for cold such as D'Cold, Vicks 
Action 500, Actified and Coldarin contain Phenyl-propanoamine (PPA), an 
ingredient that could lead to stroke; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof and whether any study has been conducted by 
Government on these drugs and if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMDOSS): (a) and (b) Phenylpropanolamine (PPA) has been commonly used as 
a nasal decongestant in cough and cold remedies in many countries including India. 
On the basis of a study conducted in Yale University, the PPA containing 
products were, withdrawn in USA in November, 2000, b ecause of reported 
risk of Hemorrhagic Stroke. However, in USA, PPA was also being used in 
higher strengths as an appetite suppressant in dietary weight loss medications. 
The matter concerning reported hemorrhagic risk of PPA was also 
examined in the same ye ar by the Committee on safety of Medicines of UK 
and it concluded that since evidence of  link between Hemorrhagic Stroke and 
PPA is weak, the formulations for cough and cold in low doses may continue to 
be sold in UK through the Pharmacies. Unlike in USA, the drug was not 
marketed for weight loss in UK. 
Issues concerning safety of PPA were also examined in 2000-01 in India in 
consultation with the Experts and further by the Drug Technical Advisory 
Board (DTAB), a statutory body under the Drugs & Cosmetics 
12 

[4 March, 2005]                       RAJYA SABHA 
Act. The experts were of the opinion that in view of the similarity in the 
pattern of use of PPA formulations in India with that in UK, the drug could be 
permitted to be marketed in cough and cold preparations with daily dose of 
not more than 50 mg. for children and 100 mg. for adults. 
PPA in cough and cold remedies continues to be used in UK, Germany etc. 
However, a fresh review of the use of PPA in anti cold preparations in context 
of the recent technical literature available on the drug, has been in itiated in 
consultation with members of National Pharmacovigilance Advisory Committee 
and other experts.

(a) whether it is a fact that only 1 .5 per cent growth has been achieved as against the

(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps Government propose to take for increasing agricultural production? 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
14 

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) 
According to the data released by Central Statistical Organization (CSO)], the 
growth rate in agriculture, including allied sectors for forestry and logging, and 
fishing, was negative (-7%) in 2002-2003 while it was 9.6% in 2003-2004. According 
to advance estimates released by the CSO, growth rate in agricluture, including 
allied sectors, in 2004-05 is 1.1%. The average annual growth rate for the first three 
years of the Tenth Plan works out to 1.2%. 
(b) Since about 60 per cent of the net so wn area is rain-fed, agricultural 
production is heavily influenced by rainfall. The year 2002-03 witnessed a severe 
drought that affected several States in the country. The favourable rainfall from 
the southwest monsoon in 2003-04 boosted agricultural production. 
However, the rainfall from the south-west monsoon in the year 2004-05 was 
deficient across time and space. Though the deficiency in rainfall from the south-
west monsoon in 2004 was less serious than that in 2002 both for the whole 
season and for the agriculturally important month of July, the kharif crop 
production in 2004-05 was adversely affected by deficient rainfall. 
(c) With a view to increasing agricultural production, the Government have 
identified thrust areas for focuse d and priority attention, which 
include agricultural credit, irrigation, horticulture, and marketing 
reforms. The Union Budget for 2005-06 has underscored the importance of 
efforts aimed at turning the focus of co mmercial banks, regional rural banks 
and co-operative banks towards providing credit, especially production credit, 
to farm households. The other areas highlighted in the Budget include micro 
irrigation technology comprising drip and sprinkler irrigation, National 
Horiticulture Mission with focus on backward and forward linkages, and 
development/strengthening of agricultural marketing infrastructure, grading and 
standardization.

*75. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY : Will the Minister of

(a) whether it is a fact that in certain cases the ignorance of the doctors results

25

(b) the measures adopted by the medical authorities to control spread of HIV virus and

(c) if so, the action taken, so far? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) As per Drugs and Cosmetic Rules, it is mandatory for all licensed 
blood banks to screen every unit of donated blood for HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, 
Syphilis and Malaria before the same is issued for transfusion to the patients. Also it is 
mandatory for all blood banks to obtain a license from the Drug Control Authorities, 
who, before issue of the license, ensures that the blood banks have the requisite 
infrastructure to carry out all the mandatory tests for safe blood. Periodic checks are 
carried out by the Drug Controller during the validity of license and before renewal. 
2. Further, in order to control the spread of HIV/AIDS, the Government is 
implementing a National AIDS Control Programme as a Centrally sponsored scheme in 
all the States and Union Territories through 38 State AIDS Control societies which also 
include 3 Municipal AIDS Control Societies in Ahmedabad, Chennai and Mumbai. 
Various steps in the Medical domain taken by Government under this programme to 
control the spread of HIV/AIDS are given hereunder:- 
(i) About 5 lakhs health care providers have been trained on HIV/AIDS. 
(ii) Services are being provided for Voluntary Counselling and Testing, treatment of 
Sexually Transmitted Disease (STDs) and Opportunistic infections through most of 
the district hospitals and States have been aksed to extend these services in every 
district. NACO is also committed to support at least one Government blood bank in 
every district of the country. 
(iii) To ensure that safe blood is provided to patients, voluntary blood donation is 
being promoted across the country. Rational use of blood is also being promoted by 
training clincians on proper indications for blood transfusion and also by setting up 
Blood Component Separation Units for providing blood components. 
(iv) Facilities for prevention of parent to child transmission have been 
26

created in 288 antenatal clinics at medical colleges and district hospitals, most 
of which are located in high prevalence States. 
(v) Free anti retroviral treatment is also being provided to AlDS patients who report to

manner. 
All these activities are carried out in collaboration with State Governments, 
Inter-sectoral partners and the Private Sector.

changes in the relative share of secondary and tertiary sectors vis-avis the 
primary sector in GDP. In 2002-03, the first year of the Tenth Plan, the growth 
rate in agriculture including the allied sectors of forestry and logging and fishing 
suffered from a sharp decline in growth by 7.0 per cent on account of severe 
drought that seriously affected several States in the country. In 2003-04, the 
second year of the Tenth Plan, agriculture including allied sectors grew at a high

base in 2003-04, has contributed to the modest growth of GDP in 2004-05.

471. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Minimum Support Price (MSP) announced by the Cotton 
Corporation of India (CCI) for cotton is remunerative for the farmers;

(c) whether the MSP is reviewed periodically and if so, the details thereof; and 
49 

 
RAJYA SABHA [4 March, 2005] 
(d) whether farmers in the cotton growing areas are taken into confidence while determining 
the MSP and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE. MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) The main objective of price policy for agricultural 
produce is to ensure remunerative prices to the growers for their produce. The Government 
decides on the MSPs for various agricultural commodities, including cotton, taking into 
account the recommendations of Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices 
(CACP), the views of State Governments and concerned Central Ministries as well as 
such other relevant factors, which in the opinion of the Government, are important for fixation 
of MSPs. The MSPs are uniform throughout the country. In addition to cost of production, 
CACP considers several other relevant factors like trends in production and productivity of 
different crops across States, demand-supply situation, price trends both at home and abroad, 
terms of trade between agriculture and non-agriculture sectors, need for crop 
diversification, resource use efficiency and food security. 
The C2 cost (actual expenses incurred in cash and kind, rent for leased-in land and imputed 
value of wages of family labour, rent for owned land and interest on fixed capital) of 
production of cotton projected by the CACP for major States for 2004-05 ranges from Rs. 1455 
to Rs. 2463 per quintal. The weighted average C2 cost of production works out to Rs. 
2021 per quintal. Since MSPs do not necessarily exceed the weighted average C2 cost in 
respect of all crops/States, the price policy seeks to ensure that the A2+FL cost (actual 
expenses in cash and kind incurred in production 4 rent paid for leased-in land + imputed 
value-of family labour) is covered by MSP in high cost/less endowed States the A2+FL cost

472. SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) the name of competent authority to decide Minimum Support Price for cotton;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) The Government decides the Minimum Support Prices 
(MSPs) for various agricultural commodities, including cotton, taking into account the 
recommendations of the Commission for Agricultural Costs & Prices (CACP), the views of 
the State Governments and the concerned Centra! Ministries as well as such, other relevant 
factors, which In the opinion of the Government, are important for fixation of MSPs. 
(b) The Cotton Corporation of India (CCI) has commenced MSP operations in all 
cotton growing States. As on February 28,2005 the CCI has purchased 122.26 lakh quintals 
of kapas (equivalent to 23.75 lakh lint bales) under MSP operations. According to the 
information furnished by the CCI, procurement under MSP operations may be in the 
range of 28 to 30 lakh lint bales during 2004-05 cotton season (October 2004— 
September 2005). As regards 2005-06 season, the CCI has indicated that it is too early 
to make an assessment of the quantity of cotton to be procured by them. In Maharashtra, 
the Maharashtra State Cooperative Cotton Growers Marketing Federation (MSCCGMF), 
under the Monopoly Procurement Scheme of the State Government has purchased kapas at 
guaranteed prices, which are higher than the MSP. The MSCCGMF has so far purchased 
38.40 lakh lint baies under the Monopoly Procurement Scheme in the State. Keeping in 
veiw the need to avoid distress sale by cotton farmers, recently the Government have declared 
National Agricultural Cooperative marketing Federation of India Limited (NAFED) as an 
agency to undertake cotton procurement, in addition to CCI. However, it is too early to 
make assessment of Use quantity likely to be procured by NAFED.

492. SHRI T.T.V DHINAKARAN: W ill the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that nearly five lakh metric tonnes of damaged 
foodgrains were disposed off during the last three years;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (DR. AKHILESH PRASAD 
SINGH): (a) A total quantity of 4 92 lakh MTs of damaged foodgrains was 
disposed of by the FCI during the years 2001-02 to 2003-04.

natural calamities like rains, floods, cyclones, etc. However, the damaged 
foodgrains constitute only a negligible percentage of the total foodgrains 
procurement for the Central Pool.

agencies and other bonafide users of such foodgrains and private parties

foodgrains were also released to the State Governments, Animal Welfare Board of 
India and Goshalas in drought hit Slates as cattle feed free of cost.

Sub: Guidelines for diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes under the Forest 
(Conservation) Act, 1980-General approval under Section-2 of Forest 
(Conservation) Act, 1980, thereof. 
Sir, 
Central Government believes that development and conservation should go hand in hand. 
This is a constitutional requirement of a welfare State like India which has also been 
emphasized by the Supreme Court from time to time. The tenet is embodied in the spirit 
of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, Awareness among the people for conservation of 
environment is bound to come from within, provided the other developmental requirements of 
food, fibre, education, health, and communication etc., are satisfied. Central Government 
is committed to expedite its efforts for developmental activities in forest areas to cover the 
largest possible population of tribal and forest dwellers. To tackle the problems of 
sensitive areas on socioeconomic front, the Central Government is all set to facilitate 
speedier execution of essential developmental activities. 
Government of India is of the view that development of tribal villages/ forest fringe 
villages can be ensured by providing basic and essential developmental facilities and 
sense of security in sensitive areas without compromising on environmental considerations 
and a balance has to made between the economic/developmental considerations on one 
hand and 
90 

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
ecological considerations on the other. It is imperative that for the creation of these 
facilities in forest/forest fringe area, most of the land requirement would have to 
be met from the forest lands. 
A small beginning in this direction has been made when general approval under 
Section 2 of Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, was accorded for underground 
laying of electricity cables and electric wires to individual households, 
drinking water supply/water pipelines, telephone lines was accorded under 
certain conditions vide para (iii) of the Guidelines of the this Ministry's letter 
No.2-1/2003-FC dated 20-10-2003, which is reproduced as under: 
"In the tribal areas, there shall be general approval under Section-2 of the 
Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 for underground laying of electricity cables 
and electric wires to individual households, drinking water supply/ water 
pipelines, telephone lines, which involves felling of trees not exceeding 50 number per 
project (should be below 60 cm. girth class) and are outside National Parks or 
Wildlife Sanctuary and are laid along the roads and within the exisitng right of 
way. This general approval shall be subject to the condition that the Nodal 
Officer shall certify compliance. Records of such works undertaken shall be 
maintained by the Nodal Officer and the Territorial DFO, Nodal Officer shall 
send quarterly report to concerned Chief Conservator of Forests (Regional 
Office) for monitoring purpose. In lieu of felling of trees, five times of the 
number of felled trees shall be planted by the User Agency at or near the site. 
Any deviation, shall require permission from the Central Government under the 
Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980." 
The issue of according general a pproval in case of some critical 
developmental and security related activities has again been reviewed by the 
Ministry of Environment and Forests holistically, and it has been found 
appropriate that extension of approval for some other critical developmental and 
other initiatives meant for people's welfare and security, will go a long way in 
educating the masses, generating awareness and seeking their cooperation in 
conservation, regeneration and restoration of degraded forest and creation of a 
sense of security among them. 
In view of the above, and in addition to general approval already given for certain 
activities as stated above, the Central Government, hereby conveys its general 
approval under section-2 of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 for diversion of 
forest land to Government Departments for following activities:

Sub:-Traditional rights of tribals on forest lands-discontinuance of eviction 
of tribals thereof. 
Sir, 
All over the world, forestry, as a land-use, has survived on the concept of sustained yield 
which was ensured by creating compatible legal systems. In India, consolidation of forest laws 
started during the British period with the inception of Indian Forest Department in 1864 and 
scientific management of forests was introduced for planned and systematic management of 
the forests. The British Government enacted the first law on forests in 1865. To 
consolidate the law relating to forests, the transit of forest produce and other related matters, 
the Indian Forest Act was enacted in 1927. According to the Indian Forest Act, 1927, the 
Government can constitute any forest land or waste land which is the property of 
Government or over which the Government has proprietary rights, a reserved forest, by issuing a 
notification to this effect Commercial interests of the then British Government motivated it to 
declare more and more lands as reserved forests, without ascertaining the rights of the 
tribals and other forest dwellers. 
100 

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Even after independence in 1947, during the process of amalgamation of princely States, 
the activity of consolidation of Government forests continued. The State Govemment/UT 
Administrations proclaimed the lands of ex-princely States and the zamindari-lands as 
Reserved Forests. However, no effective steps were taken to simulaneously settle the rights 
of tribals and other forest dwellers. Absence of records of rights which never existed for 
these people, became the main constraint in resolving this issue. As a result, the rural people, 
especially tribals and forest dwellers who have been living in the forests since time immorial, 
have come to be erroneously looked upon as encroachers of forest lands. 
The burning human problem on non-recognition of tribal rights over land with its 
origin in faulty implementation of legal provisions in pre-independent India, and 
the same remaining unresovled even after independce, has, continued to attract 
public attention. Having acknowledged the gravity of the problem, the 
Government, has been contemplating ways and means to address it. Consequently, 
for the first time, the guidelines under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 showed 
the way for legal solutions to the long pending unresolved problem of settlement of 
rights and the tribals and other forest dwellers living on the forest lands since time 
immemorial. Side by side, recognition of the concept of sustainable forest 
management through participatory approach, in the National Forest Policy, 1988, 
brought to the fore mutual interdependence of forests and people. Unlike the 1952 
Forests Policy which centred around production and commercial forestry, the 
Policy of 1988 gives due regard to the traditional rights of the tribal people on forest 
land. While recognizing the symbiotic relationship between the tribal people and 
forests, it also safeguards the customary rights and interests of the tribal people and 
forests dwellers on forest lands. 
To fulfil the commitments as enshrined in the National Forest Policy, 1988, in respect 
of settlement of people's rights, especially rights of tribals and forest dwellers, over forests 
lands in regulated manner, the Centra) Government on 18th September 1990 issued 
guidlines for settlement of disputed claims of tribals, which were reiterated on 30-10-2002, 
requesting State/UT Governments to consider the settlement of disputed claims of tribals 
over forest lands and to set up Commission/Committees at the district levels involving 
Revenue, Forests and Tribal Welfare Departments for the settlement of disputed claims of 
tribals and forest dwellers. The 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [4 March, 2005] 
State Governments/UT Administrations were also requested to submit proposals in this 
regard to enable the Central Government to take a final decision in the .matter in a time 
bound manner. However, the State/UT Governments could not implement the guidelines 
effectively and the issue remained unresolved. 
The situation of the tribals became more vulnerable when, in pursuance of the 
Hon'ble Supreme Court order dated 23-11-2001 in IA No. 703 in IA No. 502 in Writ 
Petition (C) No. 202 of 1995, the Central Government instructed all the State/UT 
Governments on 3rd May, 2002 to evict the ineligible encroachers and all post-1980 
encroachers from forests lands in a time bound manner. Consequent follow up action 
by the State/UT Governments for evicting the ineligible encroachers, brought more 
intensely to the forefront, the issue of the disputed claims and rights of the genuine 
tribals and forest dwellers. They could not be distinguished from encroachers, and 
were proceeded against. This generated much consternation. Various organizations 
took up the case of such tribals and forest dwellers whose disputed claims had not 
been enquired into, and who were being proceeded against and evicted. This prompted the 
Central Government to issue a clarification on 30-10-2002 to the effect that there is 
no change, in the policy of the Ministry with regard to regularisation of pre-1980 eligible 
encroachments, and the commitment with reference to forest-tribal interface on the 
disputed settlement claims remained valid. 
The Central Government in its continuous bid to settle the disputed claims of the 
tribals and the forest dwellers, and to legitimize their traditional rights over forest lands, of 
subsistence agriculture, and trade in MFP issued supplementary guidelines on 5-2-2004 
to encourage the State Governments/UT Administrations to take up the matter of 
settlement of rights of tribals and forest dwellers in the right earnest and perspective. 
However, before action could start on these guidelines, their operation was stayed by the 
Appex Court ex-parte on 23-2-2004. Central Government has moved an application before 
the Apex Court vacation of the order. 
After a critical examination of the issue of settlement of claims over forest lands 
and eviction of in-eligible encroachers of forest lands, what emerges is that the State/UT 
Governments were not able to distinguish between the encroachers, and the original 
tribals and other forest dwellers living on forest lands since time immemorial. 
The Central 
102 

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Government is convinced that the difficulty in distinguishing between genuine 
tribals/forest dwellers and in-eligible encroachers by the State Governments/UT 
Administrations is the main cause of the problems of tribals. Therefore, some kind of interim 
measures are necessary to safeguard the interests of the tribals and forest dwellers who have 
been living in forests since long, and whose disputed claims are yet to be settled. 
In view of the above, and without prejudice to Supreme Court's order dated 23-11 -2001 
and 23-2-2004, it has been found appropriate to request the State/UT Governments, that as an 
interim measures, they should not * resort to the eviction of tribal people and forests 
dwellers other than ineligible croachers, till the complete survey is done for the 
recognition of such people and their rights, after setting up of District Levei Committees 
involving a Deputy Collector, a Sub-Divisional Forest Officer, and a representative of 
Tribal Welfare Department, by the State/UT Governments as reiterated in guidelines dated 18-
09-1990 and 30-10-2002 of the Central Government. The State/UT Governments are advised to 
exclude such tribals/ forest dwellers, other than ineligible encroachers, from the eviction drives. 
Simultaneously, it is also clarified here that this interim measure does not stop the State/UT 
Governments from evicting the ineligible encroachers from forest lands. 
Suitable instructions may be issued to forest functionaries at all levels to keep the 
aforesaid in view while dealing with eviction of ineligible encroachments from 
forest lands.

518. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state:

under the Biodiversity Act; 
(b) what protection Government are providing on the rights of the community 
representatives; 
(c) whether any additional rules have been formulated for the Biodiversity Management 
Committees; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS 
(SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) As per Para 1 of Section 41 of the Biological 
Diversity Act, 2002, every local body shall constitute a Biodiversity Management 
Committee within its area for the purpose of promoting conservation, sustainable use and 
documentation of biological diversity including preservation of habitats, conservation of land 
races, folk varieties and cultivation, domesticated stocks and breeds of animals and micro 
organism and chronicling knowledge relating to biological diversity. 
(b) As per Section 14 of the Biological Diversity Rules, 2004, the National Biodiversity 
Authority shall consult local bodies before granting any permission for access to 
biological resources and associated knowledge to any user agency. The community 
representatives can exercise their wisdom and rights while consenting or disagreeing to 
any such request. 
(c) and (d) Rules under the Act have also been framed and duly notified. The same were 
placed on the Table of the Rajya Sabha on 23rd July, 2004 and on the Table of the Lok Sabha 
on 19th July, 2004. These rules also contained provisions relating to the Biodiversity 
Management Committee.

World Bank Report on Maternal Mortality Rate and AIDS 
532. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed a recent study of the World Bank on social 
progress and outlook highlighting inter-alia despite increase in public health expenditure the 
maternal mortality has worsened, going up from 424 per 1,00,000 in 1990s to540 per 
1,00,000 in 2000 and HIV infected has risen from 3.5 million in 1990s to 4 million in 
2000; 
(b) if so, the reaction of Government thereto; and 
(c) whether any fresh steps have been taken to upgrade the health facilities available 
to common citizens and strategy drawn up to effectively contain HIV virus already 
threatening large parts of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) The National Family 
Health Survey-! (NFHS-i). 1991-92 estimated the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) for India at 
424 per 1,00,000 live births. The National ' Family Health Survey-ll in 1997-98 estimated the 
MMR as 540 per 1,00,000 live births. The World Bank Group in their publication 'Country 
Strategy for India-September, 2004' have mentioned that based on the existing data, the 
Maternal Mortality Rate has worsened. They have, however, qualified this statement to the 
effect that there are problems with the data for this 
117 

RAJYA SABHA [4 March, 2005] 
indicator in some of the largest States that raise questions regarding data at the national levei. 
The Report of National Family Health Survey-!! also acknowledges that the difference in 
the estimates of MMR of NFHS-I and NFHS-II is not statistically significant due to 
various reasons such as large sampling errors etc. The Sample Registration System (SRS) 
of the Registrar Genera! of India have estimated the MMR for the country as 407 per 1,00,000 
live births in 1998 which is the same period when NFHS-il have estimated the MMR as 
540 per 1,00,000 live births. It is thus not correct to say that the maternal mortality rate 
has worsened 
it is true that the estimated number of HIV infections in the country has risen from 3.5 
million infections in 1998 to 51 million infections in 2003. Reasons for rise in HIV 
positive persons are low awareness of people about HIV/AIDS in the country especially 
rural and female partners in the highly vulnerabie States; high proportion of migrant 
population; inadequate safe sex practices; and large number of vulnerable population. 
National AIDS Control Organization c onducted National Ba seline General 
Population behavioral surveillance survey in 2001. The finding revealed that 76% of the 
respondent have heard of HIV/AIDS and 46.8% of respondents were aware of two 
important methods of prevention and transmission, 11.8% of males and 2% of females 
reported sex with non-regular partner while 51.2% among males and 39.8% among 
females reported using condoms during the last sex with their non-regular sax partners. 
(c) In order to prevent and control the spread of HIV/AIDS in India, Government 
has launched a comprehensive National AIDS Control Programme, currently under 
implementation throughout the country as a Centrally sponsored scheme with following 
components:— 
- Preventive interventions for high-risk populations through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy including peer 
counselling and behaviour change; 
  - Preventive interventions for the general population through programmes for 
blood safety, voluntary counselling and testing services, Prevention of Parent to 
Child, Transmission (PPTCT), Information Education and Communication 
(IEC); 
- Provision of low cost care and support services by providing 
118 

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
community care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and 
prevention of occupational exposure; 
- Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including workplace Interventions and public private partnerships; 
- Build technical and managerial capacities for programme 
implementation through surveillance, training, monitoring and 
evaluation, technical resource gr oups, operational research and 
programme management. 
In order to accelerate decline of Maternal Mortality Rate, provision has been 
kept for upgrading Primary Health Centres for providing 24-hour delivery 
services, operationaiising the First Referral units for providing Emergency 
Obstetric Care and training the heaith staff for providing Skilled Birth 
Attendance at delivery, under t he Second Phase of Reproductive and Child

Use of banned drugs 
537. SHRI ANAND KISHORE YADAV: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that some common medicines that have been banned in many 
foreign countries are still allowed to be used in India; 
(b) if so, the number and details of such medicines; 
(c) the effect of using such banned medicines; and 
(d) the action taken/being taken by Government against such companies that are still 
producing these medicines? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI RANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (d) There is no system of 
global banning of drugs. Drugs withdrawn in some countries may continue to be used in 
other countries and the decision to ban a drug in a country rests on various factors such as 
disease pattern in a country, the varying reactions of certain ethnic groups in a given 
population to the drug, the availability of safer substitutes as well as the cost factor involved 
in the treatment of the disease. 
There is an adequate mechanism to review the status of the drugs in India as and when

Population explosion and food 
543. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that population of country has crossed one thousand 
million; 
(b) whether it is a fact that due to over population despite the efforts of Government, 
common man is not getting the basic facilities of food, cloth and shelter; and 
(c) if so, the efforts made by Government to check the increasing population and 
the results thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) It is admitted that growing population causes a strain on natural and 
civic resources of the country. 
Various steps have been taken to stabilize the population of the country. The National 
Population Policy (NPP) has been adopted by Government in 2000. The National 
Commission on Population (NCP) has been constituted under the Chairmanship of the 
Prime Minister to monitor the implementation of the National Commission on Population. 
The National Population Stabilisation Fund (NPSF), i.e. Janasankhya Sthirata Kosh 
(JSK) has been set up as an autonomous body with a corpus of Rs. 100 crore to promote 
peoples' involvement in Family Welfare Programme. An Empowered Action Group 
(EAG) has been constituted in the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare under the 
Chairmanship of the Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare to give focused 
attention to the 8 demographically weaker Slates. The Reproductive and Child Health 
(RCH) Programme was launched by Government in 1997 for provision of 
reproductive, maternal, child health and contraceptive services to the people. More recently, the 
Government has decided to launch a National Rural 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
142 

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Health Mission to provide comprehensive integrated primary health services throughout the 
country. 
The demographic indicators of the country have improved considerably. The Total 
Fertility Rate has declined from 6 in 1951 to 3.2 in 1999. The Infant Mortality Rate has 
declined from 146 in 1951 to 64 per thousand population. The Maternal Mortality Ratio 
has declined from 437 in 1992 to 407 per lakh live births. The decadal growth rate of 
population has declined from 24.66% (1981) to 21.34% (2001). Similarly, Annual Growth 
Rate of population has declined from 2.22% (1981) to 1.93% (2001).

manufacturing and sale of spurious and harmful sub-standard drugs; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) As per the feedback available 
from the State Drug Controllers, 38824,43138,40862 drug samples were tested during the 
period 2001 -2002,2002-2003 and 2003-2004, out of which 96,129 and 118 samples 
declared spurious and 3458, 3724 and 3499 samples declared sub-standard 
respectively. Therefore, 0.33 per cent, 0.29 per cent and 0.288 per cent of these 
samples reported spurious and 8.9 percent, 8.63 percent and 8.56 percent of samples 
reported sub-standard. 
Overall the aforesaid data revealed that around 0.3 per cent of drugs 
were declared spurious and around 8.5- 9 per cent drugs were declared as 
sub-standard. It may be relevant to mention that a drug may be declared 
sub-standard because of defects wh ich may not affect the therapeutic 
efficacy of the drug. , 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) Manufacture of spurious/counterfeit/fake drugs is primarily a clandestine 
activity and trading in counterfeit products, including drugs, is reported world over. 
However, keeping in view the serious implications of spurious drugs on public health as well 
as the loss to genuine industry, the Government has taken the following measures to combat 
this menace:— 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
158 

[4 March, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(i) Detailed guidelines have been issued to the State Government to undertake focussed 
surveillance over possible movement of spurious drugs. 
(ii) A Capacity Building Project through World Bank assistance has been taken up to 
provide substantial assistance to State Government to upgrade drug testing facilities 
or to establish new drug testing laboratories. It is expected to increase the number of 
samples tested in the country from about 36,000 samples to 1,00,000 samples per 
year and to reduce the reporting time to less than a month as against the present period 
from 3 to 6 months. In addition, the project envisages extensive training of the Centra! 
and State/UT drug regulatory staff and the concerned personnel from the 
Pharmaceutical Industry and a campaign for Information, Education and 
Communication (IEC) for the consumers. 
(iii) Specific training programmes for reguiatory officials of State Government 
on logistics of intelligence work, prosecutions etc. has been conducted with the 
assistance of FDA, Maharashtra. This activity is proposed to be continued. 
(iv) In order to ensure efficient information exchange between drug regulatory 
officers in the country, in respect of licensing, sampling, prosecution, etc., a 
countrywide computer networking project has been undertaken by the Central 
Government This will enable the Central Government to regularly monitor the 
enforcement activities and recommend corrective measures. 
(v) Pharma industry and traders have been motivated to fight the menace of spurious drugs 
as a shared responsibility. A number of cases could be successfully detected 
through the initiative taken by pharma industry involving hiring of retired intelligence 
officers. 
(d) Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, the responsibility for regulating the 
manufacture and sale of drugs including taking legal action against the unscrupulous 
persons rests with the State Governments. As per the feedback available from the State 
Drug Controllers, 538,449 and 570 prosecutions were launched and 171,105 and 166 cases

New Molecule on AIDS Treatment 
570. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the medical faculty and Scientist in the 
University of Geneva have developed a new molecule called PSC-RANTES which 
protects against HIV/AIDS virus; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the manner in which the new molecule would help in AIDS control? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. 
PSC-RANTES is a synthetic protein. PSC-RANTES was created in a 
laboratory at the University of Geneva. There was a template: RANTES, a human 
protein that is produced in small quantities in our body. In the event of infection, 
RANTES stimulates white cells by binding to a receptor CCR5 on the cell 
membrane. In 1996 it was discovered that HIV also uses the CCR5 receptor to 
infect the cells involved in our immune system. In effect, CCR5 and RANTES race 
for the same receptor, when RANTES gets there first, HIV cannot infect the cell. 
However, despite this natural barrier, RANTES is not tough enough to fight 
off HIV infection altogether. So, in 1997 Prof. Robin Offord, Dr. Oliver 
Hartley and their team from the Department of Structural Biology and 
Bioinformatics in Geneva decided to tinker with the protein a structure in an 
attempt to make it more effective against infection. Seven years later, they 
achieved their goal by introducing chemical modification to only three amino 
acids in the original protein sequence. 
PSC-RANTES has the capability to block HIV infection. The idea is to use 
PSC-RANTES as a microbicide, in the from of a kind of cream. No conclusive 
clinical research has been carried out till now. Appropriate safety and efficacy 
studies are required. 
169 

RAJYA SABHA [4 March, 2005] 
(C) Topical microbicides that effectively block interactions between 
CCR5+immature Langerhans calls (LC) residing within genital epithelia and R5 human 
immunodeficiency virus (HIV) may decrease sexual transmission of HIV.

The Corporate Safety Plan of Indian Railways for the period 2003—2013 has been

(b) Yes, Sir. Replacement of overaged signalling systems at 1494 stations

Railways. Railway undertakes repair, rehabilitation/ rebuilding of bridges on the basis of 
their physical condition as ascertained during annual inspections and not on the basis of age.

(a) whether it is a fact that Government have set a target to instal the 110 million

said period has also been made;

sector was deregulated, delicenced and decontrolled in 1991-92. Thereafter, the market 
determines production targets and investment decisions in the steel sector. Nonetheless, 
it has been estimated that in order to become self reliant and globally competitive in the 
steel sector the country would require indigenous production of over 100 million tonnes steel 
per annum by 2020 from the 2004 level of 35 million tonnes.

2019-20, it is estimated that the industry would need fresh capital to the tune of Rs.

the existing facilities.
